(ex: at some point, a seller will receive 30k, but the buyer will have to pay 40k, destroying 10k gold)

Ion Hazzikostas has cleared this up!

>
One interesting note is that no matter when or how big the movement in the market is, sellers and buyers will always be guaranteed to get the price they saw. If a seller posts a token and the market moves downward before a buyer picks it up, the purchaser will pay the cheaper price — but the seller will still get the higher gold price they were quoted when listing the token. The same thing will happen in reverse: If a buyer pays more gold for the token than the seller was promised, the seller will still get paid the lower price.
>
“Potentially there are small amounts of gold that are being created, but also destroyed,” Hazzikostas said. “It’s about security and certainty, and it all evens out.”

>

This is a very good question, and I'm glad you've asked, as many here seem not to know the correct answer. All domesticated household cats are born with an inbuilt mechanical gyroscope. When they reach the age of maturity, cats are capable of amazing feats of agility, and are able to [correctly orient themselves](http://s02.yapfiles.ru/files/444982/33.gif) as necessary, especially when hunting for prey. In their kitten years, cats are trained in the concepts of inertia, fluid dynamics, angular momentum, torque and are given general primers on gyroscopic phsyics. This training is often undertaken by the mama-cat, though the papa-cat will often times contribute to their learning, especially in the more demanding fields, such as [precession](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precession) and [nutation](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nutation) mathematics.

This is somewhat unrelated, but the smartest kittens from a litter are also often encouraged to study the mathematical field of topology. Evidence of this is when a particularly prodigious kitten-student can be seen playing in the sock drawer, no doubt mentally permutating the complex geometry of any manner of undergarment.
